description: The measured feature topology of the Uzbekistan hydrography, declared rather than expanded. Each entry becomes one relationship-table Distribution carrying its predicate, its subject and object types and its measured row count, so the graph knows the links exist and what they mean without holding hundreds of thousands of rows a curator would never review. Ownership follows the subject where the subject is one dataset's features: a reach-to-basin table belongs to the river dataset, not the basin dataset. Where a table's subjects span many datasets, as the atlas overlay does, it belongs to the reference it was measured against.

tables.label: River reach downstream routing
tables.note: Native HydroRIVERS NEXT_DOWN, restricted to reaches inside the selection. target_scope separates a reach that routes to another selected reach from an outlet and from one whose target lies outside Uzbekistan.

tables.label: River reach to level-12 basin
tables.note: The join that makes basins the reference frame. basin_scope records a reach whose basin is outside the published reference rather than dropping the row, which is how 3,073 orphaned reaches went unnoticed before.

tables.label: Water body to level-12 basin
tables.note: Resolved from the lake's pour point, falling back to its centroid. Spatial containment, not a native field of HydroLAKES.

tables.label: Basin downstream routing, levels 01-12
tables.note: Native HydroBASINS routing for every level of the extraction, with the scope of each target recorded against the selection.

tables.label: Basin nesting across levels
tables.note: Child to parent at adjacent levels, matched by Pfafstetter prefix and confirmed by spatial overlap. Every child resolves to exactly one parent.

tables.label: Pfafstetter code nesting
tables.note: The same nesting expressed in Pfafstetter codes rather than basin identifiers. Kept separate because the identifier scheme differs, so the two tables are not directly joinable.

tables.label: Environmental atlas layers by level-12 basin
tables.note: A measured overlay of every atlas package that has published vector geometry onto the basin reference, with overlap area for polygons, length for lines and a feature count for points. This is what lets a basin id reach the atlas: before it, the 134 packages were pinned to the country and nothing finer. Raster packages with only a PNG preview are absent until PIPELINES/raster_to_geojson.py gives them geometry; the manifest names them.

tables.label: Atlas raster surfaces read per level-12 basin
tables.note: Zonal statistics for every atlas package whose raster is georeferenced and carries a single data band: pixels, mean, min, max, stddev, and majority where the surface is categorical. Read value_kind first — mean describes a continuous surface, majority a classified one, and the mean of class codes means nothing. The rasters live inside an ESRI File Geodatabase within each 7-zip layer package, which is why the TIFF-only converter never found them. Seven packages are excluded and the manifest gives the reason for each: six are rendered RGB images or carry no georeference, and one is not on disk.

tables.label: Basin downstream routing, lake format, levels 01-12
tables.note: The lake-format counterpart. Lake format splits basins at lakes and therefore mints different HYBAS_IDs, so these rows are not interchangeable with the BasinATLAS ones. The delivery wrote this file with a UTF-8 byte-order mark, unlike its BasinATLAS counterpart, so it must be read with encoding utf-8-sig; plain utf-8 turns the first column name into \ufefflevel and a lookup by name raises KeyError.

tables.label: Basin nesting across levels, lake format
tables.note: Lake-format child to parent nesting, on lake-format identifiers. The delivery wrote this file with a UTF-8 byte-order mark, unlike its BasinATLAS counterpart, so it must be read with encoding utf-8-sig; plain utf-8 turns the first column name into \ufefflevel and a lookup by name raises KeyError.

tables.label: Pfafstetter code nesting, lake format
tables.note: Pfafstetter nesting for the lake-format extraction. The delivery wrote this file with a UTF-8 byte-order mark, unlike its BasinATLAS counterpart, so it must be read with encoding utf-8-sig; plain utf-8 turns the first column name into \ufefflevel and a lookup by name raises KeyError.

tables.label: Level-12 basins by province
tables.note: Level-12 basins against the 14 first-level units — provinces, the autonomous republic and Tashkent city. Each row carries the area the two share, so a traced catchment can be attributed to the provinces that feed it. Every unit resolves to a place concept in the ontology, matched by P-code because the COD spellings differ from the vocabulary's. Carries no quality column because every row is a measured geometric overlap rather than a sensor reading — there is no sentinel or scaling fault for it to record.

tables.label: Level-12 basins by district
tables.note: The same overlay at the second level, across 199 districts, independent cities and gorhokimiyat towns. This is the resolution at which water administration actually happens, and the reason the districts carry no place concept: they are features, and the schema puts features in a table. Carries no quality column because every row is a measured geometric overlap rather than a sensor reading — there is no sentinel or scaling fault for it to record.

tables.label: Land cover area by district and year
tables.note: Area of each land cover class inside each of the 199 second-level units, once per year. Measured on Earth Engine with pixelArea summed per class, so ground area is right whatever projection the reduction lands in. This is the first table in the graph with a time dimension: a row is keyed by unit, year and class together. Carries no quality column because every row is a measured geometric overlap rather than a sensor reading — there is no sentinel or scaling fault for it to record.

dimensionColumns.meaning: the calendar year the mosaic covers
land cover class code in the product's 9-class scheme

tables.label: Land cover area by level-12 basin and year
tables.note: The same measurement against the hydrological frame. Only level 12 is stored: a parent basin's land cover is the sum of its children, so the coarser levels are derivable through the Pfafstetter hierarchy and storing them as well would be twelve times the rows and a second set of numbers that could disagree with the first. Carries no quality column because every row is a measured geometric overlap rather than a sensor reading — there is no sentinel or scaling fault for it to record.

dimensionColumns.meaning: the calendar year the mosaic covers
land cover class code in the product's 9-class scheme

tables.label: CFSv2 basin monthly state
tables.note: Monthly mean of the 6-hourly CFSv2 field over each level-7 basin: precipitation, temperature, four soil-moisture depths, evaporative demand, radiation and humidity. Level 7 because the grid is 34.8 km and roughly nine and a half level-12 basins share a single pixel. Pure measurement, no interpretation.

tables.label: CFSv2 basin climatological baseline
tables.note: Mean and standard deviation per basin, calendar month and variable over a stated reference period. The period stays inside the operational CFSv2 era: the record reaches 1979, but 25 cm soil moisture steps up 1.41 standard deviations at the 2011 CFSR handover, and a baseline spanning that would bias every anomaly drawn against it. Cells with fewer than three years carry no standard deviation. Carries no quality column because it is derived: its producer reads only rows the observation table marked ok, so every row here is one by construction.

tables.label: CFSv2 basin anomaly
tables.note: Observations expressed as z-scores against the baseline, with a symmetric classification from extremely dry to extremely wet. Derived and rebuildable: it holds no measurement the other two tables do not already have, and it moves whenever the reference period is redefined. Carries no quality column because it is derived: its producer reads only rows the observation table marked ok, so every row here is one by construction.

tables.label: CHIRPS v3 basin pentadal precipitation
tables.note: Accumulated rainfall per level-12 basin per pentad — days 1-5, 6-10, 11-15, 16-20, 21-25 and 26 to month end. CHIRPS is computed pentadally and its daily series is a disaggregation: summed over a month the two agree to within 0.00%, so the daily product adds nothing and its within-pentad variation is an artefact rather than an observation. Six pentads reconstruct a month to 0.0002 mm, which is why no monthly table is stored beside this one. The days column varies because the sixth pentad runs to month end, so an mm/day rate must divide by it rather than by five. Read at level 12 rather than level 7: at this product's 5.6 km grid a level-12 basin covers about four pixels, so it carries a value of its own, and the reduction costs no more because it is priced by the raster read rather than the polygon count. CFSv2 stays at level 7 because its 34.8 km grid puts nine and a half level-12 basins inside one pixel.

tables.label: CHIRTS basin monthly temperature and humidity
tables.note: Station-blended temperature at the same 5.6 km grid as CHIRPS, reduced to monthly statistics per level-12 basin. The day counts above 35 and 40 degrees are the reason for reading a daily product: a monthly mean cannot say how many days crossed a threshold. The record is closed at 2016-12-31, so this is a historical baseline and not a monitoring layer. heat_index_max is in Fahrenheit and derived from the daily mean temperature, unlike every other column here, which is metric. Read at level 12 rather than level 7: at this product's 5.6 km grid a level-12 basin covers about four pixels, so it carries a value of its own, and the reduction costs no more because it is priced by the raster read rather than the polygon count. CFSv2 stays at level 7 because its 34.8 km grid puts nine and a half level-12 basins inside one pixel.

tables.label: CPC basin monthly temperature
tables.note: Gauge-based half-degree temperature reduced to monthly statistics per level-6 basin, with counts of hot and frost days. Level 6 because a half-degree cell at this latitude is 55.3 by 41.7 km — about 2,305 km², nearly twice a CFSv2 pixel — so a level-7 basin covers only 1.2 cells. Uniquely here the source carries its own quality signal: nmax and nmin give the stations informing each cell, and over Uzbekistan that averages 0.13 per day with 51% of basin-months seeing none at all. Those rows are marked ok-interpolated: the product is long and current, but over this country it is mostly interpolation from distant reports rather than local observation, and should be weighted accordingly against CHIRTS.

dimensionColumns.meaning: which geography the unit belongs to
the index, or the area share in one band

tables.label: Human modification by level-12 basin
tables.note: Cumulative human modification for 2016 — settlement, agriculture, transport, mining and energy, electrical infrastructure — as a 0 to 1 index at 1 km, from thirteen source datasets. Stored with the area share in each modification band beside the mean, because a mean of 0.3 describes both a uniformly semi-modified landscape and a city beside a desert. Carries no quality column: every row is a measured geometric reduction of a single complete image. The layer is timeless in the strict sense — the collection holds one image with no system:time_start — so there is nothing to refresh and no period it can fall behind. Measured over both frames because human modification belongs to whoever governs a place as much as to whatever drains it, and the frame changes the answer: over basins Uzbekistan averages 0.33, over districts 0.61, because districts are drawn around settlement while basins include the empty desert between it.

tables.label: Human modification by district
tables.note: Cumulative human modification for 2016 — settlement, agriculture, transport, mining and energy, electrical infrastructure — as a 0 to 1 index at 1 km, from thirteen source datasets. Stored with the area share in each modification band beside the mean, because a mean of 0.3 describes both a uniformly semi-modified landscape and a city beside a desert. Carries no quality column: every row is a measured geometric reduction of a single complete image. The layer is timeless in the strict sense — the collection holds one image with no system:time_start — so there is nothing to refresh and no period it can fall behind. Measured over both frames because human modification belongs to whoever governs a place as much as to whatever drains it, and the frame changes the answer: over basins Uzbekistan averages 0.33, over districts 0.61, because districts are drawn around settlement while basins include the empty desert between it.

tables.label: CAMS atmospheric composition by basin
tables.note: Monthly mean of the CAMS +0h analysis per level-6 basin: aerosol optical depth at 550 nm and PM2.5. Only these two parameters exist before 2021-07-01, so reading just them gives a record that runs the whole way back without silently changing content partway through. PM2.5 is converted from kg/m3 to micrograms per cubic metre, which is the unit air quality is discussed in. Level 6 because the 0.4 degree grid is 1,470 km2 at this latitude and a level-7 basin covers only 1.9 pixels. This is the analysis, not a forecast — see cams-forecast-skill for how much the forecasts drift from it.

tables.label: CAMS forecast skill against its own analysis
tables.note: Mean absolute error, bias and correlation between each forecast lead time and the +0h analysis valid at the same moment, over Uzbekistan. CAMS issues two five-day forecasts a day, so any moment has up to eleven images aiming at it and their disagreement is measurable from the collection alone. Read the scope carefully: this verifies forecast against analysis, and the analysis is itself a model state constrained by assimilated satellite retrievals, not a measurement. A forecast agreeing with it means the model agreed with itself. Independent verification would need surface monitors or AERONET sites, of which Uzbekistan has very few. Carries no quality column because it is derived: every row is a statistic computed over pairs the state table already accepted, and the pairs column records how many went into it, so a thin month is visible rather than hidden.
